column2: Paper
column3: Problem
column4: UQ Technique
column5: Key Results
column6: Limitations

column2: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know (Kadavath et al.)
column3: Do LLMs know when their own answers are likely correct?
column4: Self-verbalized (P(True); P(IK) is a trained value head, not verbalized text)
column5: Large models well-calibrated on MC/ T-F tasks with suitable formatting; P(True) improves with scale and with showing several own samples; RLHF policies appear miscalibrated, largely fixed by a temperature adjustment
column6: P(IK) needs fine-tuning with a value head (white-box); P(IK) calibration degrades out of distribution; mainly pretrained models and five sampling datasets

column2: Self\-Check\-GPT (Manakul, Liusie, Gales)
column3: Detect hallucinations without external knowledge base or logit access
column4: Consis\-tency-based (semantic-similarity)
column5: Prompt variant best (AUC-PR 93.42 NonFact); NLI close second (92.50), better cost/ performance trade-off; beats grey-box token-probability baselines
column6: Computationally heavy (Prompt variant); requires many samples (20); one dataset (GPT-3 WikiBio); can't catch consistent-but-wrong hallucinations (see SAC3)

column2: Semantic Uncertainty (Kuhn, Gal, Farquhar)
column3: Token-level entropy overestimates uncertainty when many phrasings share one meaning
column4: Semantic-similarity (Semantic Entropy)
column5: Beats predictive entropy, length-norm entropy, lexical similarity, P(True); gap widens with model size; temp ~0.5 optimal
column6: Hard clustering (the NLI-based equivalence is not strictly transitive, which Kuhn et al.\ acknowledge but report as not a noticeable problem in practice; SAR's authors judged ~36.7% of entailment predictions undesirable in a manual check of 120 long-answer questions); needs logits; ignores token relevance

column2: Survey of Uncertainty Estimation in LLMs: Sources, Methods, Applications, Challenges (He et al.)
column3: No prior survey organizes UQ by SOURCE (data, model, user) rather than method
column4: All (organizes token-level, Bayesian, consistency-based, conformal, single/ multi-prompt, ensembles)
column5: Introduces data/ model/ user uncertainty taxonomy; 19 open challenges incl. lack of ground-truth uncertainty scores, human meta-evaluation gap
column6: No original empirical validation; long and broad in scope; some overlap with Shorinwa taxonomy

column2: SELAUR (Zhang, Liu, Cheng, Wang, Murray, Wei)
column3: Standard RL discards failed agent trajectories entirely, wasting information
column4: Token-level (entropy, LC, margin) used as an RL reward signal, not just detection
column5: Highest scores vs PPO, RLOO, GRPO, GiGPO on both benchmarks with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, but small margins over GiGPO in several settings; combined uncertainty beats any single metric; maintains higher entropy late in training (less exploration collapse)
column6: Only tested on 2 benchmarks; requires white-box logit access; adds RL training complexity

column2: Uncertainty Quantification in LLM Agents: Foundations, Emerging Challenges, Opportunities (Oh et al.)
column3: Existing UQ assumes static single-turn inference; doesn't fit multi-turn interactive agents
column4: General framework subsuming token-level, semantic, verbalized methods as special cases
column5: Token-probability and verbalized estimators show close-to-random task-success prediction in many cases (tau2-bench, GPT-4.1/Kimi-K2.5); 4 challenges identified with preliminary numerical evidence
column6: Framework is descriptive/ position-oriented, not yet a working solution; pilot experiments are small-scale

column2: A Survey of Confidence Estimation and Calibration in LLMs (Geng et al.)
column3: No comprehensive survey systematically organizing LLM confidence/ calibration work
column4: All (logit-based, internal-state, linguistic, consistency-based, surrogate models)
column5: Organizes by generation vs. classification tasks; white-box/ black-box Venn-diagram taxonomy; explicitly notes lack of experimental benchmarks as own limitation
column6: Self-acknowledged: no original experiments; narrower scope than Shorinwa/ He surveys

column2: How Humans and LLMs Differ in Processing Uncertainty in Polarized Discourse (Donkers, Ziegler)
column3: Do LLMs perceive/ process expressed uncertainty in discourse the way humans do?
column4: Not a detection method -- studies communicative/ social uncertainty perception
column5: Both humans \
column6: LLMs detect polarized vs. moderate discourse, but LLMs amplify differences 3-6.5x; humans show cascading mediation, LLMs show independent parallel processing with no cross-construct mediation
column7: Single topic (UBI) tested; LLM-generated (not human) discourse; correlational (structural-equation) evidence, so the "architecture" reading is ours to caveat, not a causal result

column2: A Survey on Uncertainty Quantification of LLMs: Taxonomy, Open Research Challenges (Shorinwa et al.)
column3: Field lacks a taxonomy unifying disparate UQ methods considering LLM-specific architecture
column4: 4-category taxonomy: token-level, self-verbalized, semantic-similarity, mechanistic interpretability
column5: Most comprehensive method-based taxonomy of the 3 surveys; unique mechanistic-interpretability coverage; robotics + chatbot applications; 'consistency is not factuality' / 'entropy is not factuality' challenges named explicitly
column6: No original experiments; very long; mechanistic-interpretability-UQ connection still speculative

column2: Language Models Prefer What They Know (Shrivastava, Kumar, Liang)
column3: Absolute self-rated confidence (0-1) is coarse-grained and poorly discriminative
column4: Self-verbalized (relative confidence)
column5: Beats absolute/ self-consistency prompting for 4/5 models (gains about 1-6 points over direct); best rank aggregator varies by model; CoT slightly lowers AUC (87.2 to 86.8, GPT-4o)
column6: Only tested on MC QA; Claude 3.5 Sonnet is an exception; relies on many pairwise LLM calls

column2: SAC3 (Zhang, Li, Das, Malin, Kumar)
column3: Self-consistency alone misses question-level and model-level hallucinations
column4: Consis\-tency-based (extends Self\-Check\-GPT)
column5: On all-hallucinated classification data, SAC3-all (Guanaco-33b verifier) beats the SC2 self-consistency baseline by 51.2 accuracy points (99.4 vs 48.2, prime numbers); SAC3-Q alone also far exceeds SC2; SAC3-Q and SAC3-all most robust to the threshold
column6: Verifier LM choice matters a lot (verifiers refused many senator questions); extra cost from perturbation, equivalence checks and verifier calls; one target model (gpt-3.5-turbo), four datasets

column2: Kernel Language Entropy (Nikitin, Kossen, Gal, Marttinen)
column3: Semantic Entropy's hard clustering discards fine-grained similarity information
column4: Semantic-similarity (generalizes Semantic Entropy; works without token probabilities)
column5: Heat-kernel variant beats SE in 72% of 60 model-dataset scenarios by AUROC (discrete SE 77%, P(True) 83%); SE is a special case of KLE
column6: Needs multiple samples and an NLI model; kernel hyperparameters; QA and math only; token-likelihood methods do better on non-instruction-tuned models

column2: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (Xiong et al.)
column3: No systematic empirical framework compares black-box confidence-elicitation strategies
column4: Self-verbalized + consistency (unifying framework)
column5: Plain verbalized confidence is overconfident (mostly 80-100%) and near chance at failure prediction; multi-sample consistency raises AUROC (GSM8K, GPT-3.5: 54.8 to 92.7) but unevenly, and adding verbalized confidence to the aggregation beats consistency alone
column6: CoT lowers ECE largely via accuracy gains, while AUROC falls on 2 of 5 datasets (GPT-3.5); no strategy consistently best; hard on professional knowledge; single-answer QA only

column2: Shifting Attention to Relevance / SAR (Duan et al.)
column3: Entropy-based UQ treats all tokens/ sentences equally, letting irrelevant tokens dominate uncertainty score
column4: Relevance-weighted uncertainty
column5: Higher AUROC than PE, LN-PE, Semantic Entropy and Lexical Similarity in most settings (+7.1 AUROC points over SE on average, four instruction-tuned models, Rouge-L 0.5); SentSAR with 2 samples beat 5-sample baselines on SciQ/ TriviaQA
column6: Requires token logits; adds sentence-similarity overhead; not better everywhere (e.g., Rouge-L 0.3, LLaMA-13b TriviaQA; MedQA with Vicuna-13b); correctness defined by Rouge-L/ similarity thresholds; free-form QA, models $ $33B

column2: Bench\-mark\-ing UQ Methods with LM-Polygraph (Vashurin et al.)
column3: Evaluation protocols for LLM UQ differ across papers (arbitrary correctness thresholds, n-gram quality metrics, omitted simple baselines), making results hard to compare
column4: All categories (Information-based, Sample Diversity, Density-based, Reflexive)
column5: MSP strong on short outputs but lags on GSM8k and selective generation; NLI-based black-box sample-diversity methods best on long outputs; CCP best on claim-level fact-checking in 4 of 5 settings; P(True) mostly no better than random on 7B/12B base models
column6: Models are $ $13B plus GPT-4o-mini; fact-checking labels come from GPT-4 (F1 0.80-0.93 vs.\ manual on small subsets); main text compares only six methods across languages

column2: Position: UQ Needs Reassessment for LLM Agents (Kirchhof, Kasneci, Kasneci)
column3: Definitions of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty conflict and, the authors argue, lose their meaning when an agent interacts with a user
column4: Position paper: review of aleatoric/ epistemic definitions (mostly classical ML literature) and a research agenda
column5: Toy example shows definitions disagree; proposes three research directions (underspecification, interactive learning, output uncertainties) while keeping aleatoric/ epistemic for training and active learning
column6: No new method or experiments; interactive-agent argument is conceptual, not tested on agents

column2: Fact-Checking via Token-Level UQ / CCP (Fadeeva et al.)
column3: Token-probability methods conflate claim-type, surface-form, and factual-claim uncertainty
column4: Token-level (Claim-Conditioned Probability)
column5: Highest ROC-AUC vs.\ Max Probability, Perplexity, Token Entropy, P(True) in all 4 English models (+0.04 to +0.07) and most others, but margins of only 0.01 for Yi and GPT-4 (Arabic); on 100 human-labelled Vicuna-13b claims, ROC-AUC 0.78 vs.\ FactScore 0.72
column6: P(True) has higher PR-AUC on GPT-3.5-turbo (authors suggest the API's 5-alternative limit); claim splitting uses GPT models; NLI classifier untested across domains; white-box only; calibration not studied

column2: Generating with Confidence (Lin, Trivedi, Sun)
column3: Uncertainty (input-level) and confidence (response-specific) are conflated in prior black-box work
column4: Response-similarity graph (black-box)
column5: NLI-entailment similarity usually best (Jaccard/ contra\-dic\-tion variants 0-6 AUARC points lower); response-specific confidence usually beats input-level uncertainty; matches or beats SE and beats P(True) in most settings without logits, but SE wins e.g.\ LLaMA2/TriviaQA
column6: Degenerate at temperature 0 (stated by authors); SE better at temperature 0.5 with few samples; calibration set aside (appendix: histogram binning works); QA only; correctness judged by gpt-3.5-turbo; models $ $13B plus gpt-3.5-turbo

column2: Detecting Hallu\-ci\-na\-tions in LLM Generation: A Token Probability Approach (Quevedo et al.)
column3: Can four token-probability features from an evaluator LLM, fed to a small supervised classifier, detect hallucination?
column4: Token-probability features with a supervised classifier (evaluator may differ from generator)
column5: HaluEval, trained on 10% and tested on 90%: up to 0.98 (summarization) and 0.95 (QA) accuracy; baselines not rerun on the same split, and about 0.99 even without the condition text, which the authors read as a dataset pattern; trails MIND on 5 of 6 HELM generators
column6: Roughly chance on True-False; collapsed on HaluEval general queries; needs labelled data and token probabilities from an evaluator model

column2: Mitigating LLM Hallu\-ci\-na\-tions via Conformal Abstention (Yadkori et al.)
column3: Consis\-tency-based uncertainty scores lack a principled threshold for deciding when to abstain
column4: Conformal abstention (static threshold)
column5: Match-count scores abstain far less than log-probability scores on long answers (Temporal Sequences), comparable on short (TriviaQA); calibrated methods are mostly, not always, under target at small calibration sizes, with very high abstention
column6: Needs a held-out calibration set and exchangeability; one model (Gemini Pro), two datasets; guarantee is marginal and in expectation for the CRC variant; extra sampling cost

column2: Learning Conformal Abstention Policies (Tayebati et al.)
column3: Static conformal-prediction thresholds don't adapt to varying task complexity/ distribution shift
column4: Conformal prediction (learned/ adaptive, task-level)
column5: Learned policy consistently outperforms fixed-threshold conformal baselines while meeting the same coverage target
column6: Authors caution the learned policy may overfit or distort the conformal guarantee

column2: Hallu\-ci\-na\-tion Detection and Mitigation in Large Language Models (Pesaranghader, Li)
column3: Industry needs an operational, end-to-end framework connecting detection to mitigation, not just a new metric
column4: Multi-method operational framework
column5: Describes a closed feedback loop across model/ context/ data tiers; financial extraction case study lists expected benefits only
column6: No measured results at all; single case study domain (finance); own bibliography contains miscited references

column2: Adaptive Conformal Prediction for Improving Factuality (Rubashevskii et al.)
column3: Existing conformal-prediction factuality methods aren't prompt-adaptive, causing over- or under-coverage per prompt
column4: Conformal prediction (prompt-adaptive)
column5: Outperforms global-threshold conformal factuality on category-wise conditional coverage while retaining marginal coverage
column6: Very recent preprint, under review; white-box models only; theorem stated for oracle quantile

column2: From Calibration to Collaboration (Devic et al.)
column3: UQ research optimizes calibration metrics divorced from whether uncertainty actually helps human decision-making
column4: Meta-level critique of evaluation methodology across all UQ categories
column5: Argues good calibration $ $ good human-AI collaboration; identifies 3 systematic blind spots in current benchmarks/ metrics
column6: No new experiments

column2: Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words (Lin, Hilton, Evans)
column3: Token log-probability conflates uncertainty over wording with uncertainty over the underlying claim
column4: Self-verbalized (verbalized probability)
column5: GPT-3 can be fine-tuned to state calibrated confidence in words or numbers, moderately calibrated under shift; beats logit baselines on the multi-answer set only; tentative evidence of latent pre-trained features
column6: Arithmetic only, one model (GPT-3 175B); logit methods better on multiply-divide; much weaker out of distribution; supervised fine-tuning

column2: The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It's Lying (Azaria, Mitchell)
column3: Can hidden-layer activations reveal truthfulness independent of the model's own output?
column4: Mechanistic / internal-state probing
column5: About 71% (OPT-6.7B) to 83% (LLaMA-2-7B) on held-out topics of a true/ false dataset; weaker (about 61-71%) on the model's own generated statements; beats few-shot and BERT baselines (about 54-56%)
column6: Needs labeled training data and white-box access; best layer varies by model; only two 7B models, English, isolated statements

column2: Discovering Latent Knowledge in LMs Without Supervision (Burns, Ye, Klein, Steinhardt)
column3: Can a truth direction be recovered from activations with zero labels at all?
column4: Mechanistic / internal-state probing (unsupervised)
column5: 71.2% vs 67.2% calibrated zero-shot (average excluding T0); about half the prompt sensitivity; robust to misleading prompts
column6: Needs white-box access; about 12 points below the supervised ceiling (83.7%); worse than zero-shot on RoBERTa; yes-no tasks only; deception untested

column2: Detecting Hallu\-ci\-na\-tions in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy (Farquhar, Kossen, Kuhn, Gal)
column3: Can entropy over meanings detect confabulations without task-specific data, including in paragraph-length text?
column4: Semantic-similarity (semantic entropy, plus a discrete variant needing no token probabilities)
column5: Mean AUROC 0.790 over 30 task-model combinations vs 0.687-0.698 for naive entropy, P(True) and embedding regression; discrete variant beats baselines on GPT-4 biographies (150 claims, 21 people)
column6: Needs about ten samples and an entailment judge; does not catch consistent errors; clustering can over-split; no clinical or legal evaluation

column2: Semantic Entropy Probes (Kossen, Han, Razzak, Schut, Malik, Gal)
column3: Can semantic entropy be approximated cheaply, without resampling multiple full generations?
column4: Mechanistic approximation of semantic-similarity signal
column5: Near-zero test-time overhead versus 5-10 samples; generalizes better to unseen tasks than correctness-trained probes; in-distribution similar to them; below full Semantic Entropy
column6: Approximation that does not match full SE; evaluated on QA with models up to 70B; sits ambiguously between semantic and mechanistic categories

column2: Self-Contra\-dictory Hallu\-ci\-na\-tions of LLMs (Mündler, He, Jenko, Vechev)
column3: Can a model's self-contra\-dic\-tion within one generation be detected, and removed, by prompting alone?
column4: Consis\-tency-based (within-generation)
column5: 15.7-22.9% of sentences self-contradict across four models (17.7% ChatGPT); detection F1 about 80%; revision removes 76-90% of contra\-dic\-tions
column6: Roughly 80-90 times the generation tokens; weak with open-source detectors; open-domain text and short QA only

column2: Bench\-mark\-ing LLMs via Uncertainty Quantification (Ye, Yang, Pang, Wang, Wong, Yilmaz, Shi, Tu)
column3: Can conformal prediction set size rank LLMs on uncertainty as well as accuracy?
column4: Conformal prediction used as a benchmark metric (compares models, not UQ methods)
column5: Across 9 model series and 5 multiple-choice tasks: higher accuracy does not imply lower uncertainty, larger models can be more uncertain, instruction fine-tuning tends to raise uncertainty; coverage near the 90% target
column6: Multiple-choice only (free-form loses the guarantee); needs option logits or about 50 samples; calibration and test data must match

column2: Inference-Time Intervention (Li, Patel, Viégas, Pfister, Wattenberg)
column3: Can a model be steered toward truthfulness at inference time without fine-tuning?
column4: Mechanistic intervention
column5: Raises Alpaca truthfulness on TruthfulQA from 32.5% to 65.1%; needs only a few hundred labeled examples; no weight fine-tuning
column6: Needs white-box access and labeled data; truthfulness-helpfulness trade-off; mainly TruthfulQA and 7B models, small gains elsewhere

column2: Robots That Ask for Help / KnowNo (Ren, Dixit, Bodrova, Singh, Tu, et al.)
column3: When should a robot ask a human for help, given uncertainty in LLM-generated action plans?
column4: Conformal prediction (embodied/ robotics application)
column5: Statistical guarantee on task completion while minimizing human help requests (10-24% less help than baselines without formal assurances); predates #20 by about ten months
column6: Domain-specific (robotics); guarantee is over scenarios, not per episode, and assumes text-grounded environment and faithful human help

column2: Conformal Language Modeling (Quach, Fisch, Schuster, Yala, Sohn, Jaakkola, Barzilay)
column3: How can conformal prediction apply to generation, where the output space is unbounded and can only be sampled?
column4: Conformal prediction (foundational, generation-adapted)
column5: Calibrated sampling and rejection give a set that contains an acceptable answer with high probability (i.i.d., admission-function assumptions); set size minimized empirically, plus component-level guarantees
column6: Predates and is more general than later abstention-specific work

column2: UProp (Duan, Diffenderfer, Madireddy, Chen, Kailkhura, Xu)
column3: How should an agent's uncertainty at one step account for uncertainty inherited from earlier decisions?
column4: Agentic uncertainty propagation (mutual-information-based)
column5: Outperforms seven single-turn UQ baselines (average or RMS aggregation) by 2.3-11% AUROC on AgentBench-OS and StrategyQA/ HotpotQA; concrete estimator for the propagation problem Oh et al. (#6) later analyze
column6: Relies on Monte-Carlo trajectory sampling (estimates may deviate with few samples; adds latency); partly evaluated on closed-source models

column2: SAUP (Zhao, Li, Liu, Cheng, Sun, et al.)
column3: Same propagation problem as #35, via a different mechanism
column4: Agentic uncertainty propagation (situational weighting)
column5: Up to $ $0.19 AUROC over best one-step baseline (StrategyQA, LLaMA3 8B); only 0.006-0.016 on GPT-4o HotpotQA/ MMLU; plain RMS/ geometric-mean propagation already improves on one-step baselines
column6: Learned version needs manually annotated data (authors); one-step estimator errors propagate (authors); only length-normalized entropy tested; QA with ReAct, final-answer correctness only

column2: Towards Uncertainty-Aware Language Agent / UALA (Han, Buntine, Shareghi)
column3: When should an agent trust its own answer, and when should it use a tool or ask a human?
column4: Action-selection via uncertainty
column5: Vs.\ always-on ReAct: ChatGPT HotpotQA EM 32.0 to 38.2 with tool calls 2,114 to 403, over 65% fewer tokens; gain shrinks with model size; mixed vs.\ no-tool baselines (e.g., LLaMA2-70B MMLU 56.7 vs.\ 64.7 Standard); verbalised confidence worse (HotpotQA, ChatGPT only)
column6: Task-specific uncertainty method and calibration set; threshold from plain-prompt answers may not suit trajectories; QA only, few tools; human help simulated with gold answers

column2: Perceptions of Linguistic Uncertainty by LMs and Humans (Belém, Kelly, Steyvers, Singh, Smyth)
column3: Do LLMs interpret hedge words (e.g. 'probably') the way humans do, including judging another agent's uncertainty?
column4: Human-perception empirical study
column5: 7 of 10 models match population modal answers better than an individual person does, but answers are less varied than people's; for the 6 best models, mean answers are 7.0 points lower for false than true statements (humans: far smaller gap); agreement falls 4.3 points vs.\ 0.9 for humans on checkable statements
column6: 14 English expressions, US-based human reference (94 people), 60+60 statements (400 more as check); truth value is a proxy for model belief; context effects not explored; no explanation of why models acquired the ability

column2: "I'm Not Sure, But..." (Kim, Liao, Vorvoreanu, Ballard, Vaughan)
column3: Does an LLM expressing uncertainty in natural language actually change user reliance and trust?
column4: Human-perception empirical study
column5: First-person hedges lowered agreement (74.8% vs.\ 80.9%) and raised accuracy (72.8% vs.\ 63.9%) and lowered trust intention; general-perspective hedges moved the same way but not significantly; overreliance reduced, not eliminated
column6: Yes/ no medical questions, 8 per participant, U.S. Mechanical Turk workers; fictional system with 50% accuracy and hedges unrelated to correctness; first-person versus general-perspective difference significant only for trust intention

column2: Revisiting Epistemic Markers in Confidence Estimation (Liu, Zong, Wang, Song)
column3: Does the accuracy attached to the epistemic markers (e.g. 'fairly confident') an LLM uses stay stable across datasets?
column4: Self-verbalized / linguistic marker reliability
column5: 7 models, 7 datasets: cross-dataset calibration error 17.7 vs 8.2 in-distribution (numerical confidence 16.6); marker rankings unstable (rank correlation 0.21); stronger models more stable
column6: English only, short closed-form QA, idealized setting; measures the model's own marker accuracy, not human interpretation; no human participants

column2: LLMs Know More Than They Show (Orgad, Toker, Gekhman, Reichart, Szpektor, Kotek, Belinkov)
column3: Where in a generated answer is truthfulness encoded, and does a probe trained for one task transfer?
column4: Mechanistic / internal-state probing (supervised, exact answer tokens)
column5: Probe at exact answer tokens: AUC 0.85 vs.\ 0.75 (minimum token logit) and 0.74 (P(True)) on TriviaQA with Mistral-7b-Instruct; probes generalize mainly between similar tasks and rarely exceed logits alone; error types predictable from internal states
column6: Needs white-box access and labeled data per task; weak cross-task transfer; correctness labels mostly heuristic; refusals excluded; four 7-8B models

column2: Uncertainty Quantification of LLMs through Multiple Uncertainty Sources (Chen, Liu, Da, Chen, Papalexakis, Wei)
column3: Black-box UQ methods each rely on a single signal and capture one facet of uncertainty
column4: Response-similarity: stacks several sources' similarity matrices into a tensor and scores by Tucker/CP reconstruction error
column5: Higher AUROC and AUARC than the best single-source baseline in all 30 cells of the main table (e.g., CoQA, Llama2-13B AUROC: 0.7802 vs.\ 0.7566)
column6: Needs auxiliary LLMs and an NLI model (added cost); a badly wrong source can degrade the combined score; some margins very small; no variance or significance tests

column2: Judge, Retrieve, or Abstain (Badshah, Emami, Sajjad)
column3: LLM judges of factual QA err silently, and uncertainty thresholds give no control over the error rate of accepted verdicts
column4: Risk-controlled routing: predictive entropy, retrieve and re-judge, else abstain; Clopper-Pearson bound on the false discovery rate
column5: Bound held in all 32 candidate-judge-dataset combinations; at target 0.20, retrieval raised coverage 0.40 to 0.85 (HotpotQA, Llama-8B judge) and 0.07 to 0.82 (NQ-Open, Qwen-8B judge)
column6: Factual QA only; token log-probabilities needed; recalibration when task, candidate, or judge changes; data-dependent threshold search (main results uncorrected); labels mostly from an LLM evaluator; human review not implemented

column2: Not All Uncertainty Is Equal (Villavicencio, Pan, Wang)
column3: Does the granularity of displayed uncertainty change how people verify LLM answers?
column4: Human-perception empirical study: output-, step-, and word-level uncertainty displays
column5: N=192 in four conditions; word-level display raised agreement (0.730 vs.\ 0.674); step-level display cut link clicks (0.318 vs.\ 0.557); no significant accuracy differences (0.617-0.657)
column6: Uncalibrated, overconfident estimates; deliberately hard medical questions; crowdsourced U.S., English-speaking, highly educated sample

column2: Anthropomimetic Uncertainty (Ulmer, Lorson, Titov, Hardmeier)
column3: Verbalized uncertainty in LLMs ignores how humans communicate uncertainty
column4: Argument paper combining a review of 53 papers with experiments on six commercial LLMs
column5: 61% of reviewed methods use numerical expressions and 78% prompting; verbalization varies widely with model, speaker-listener relationship, and subject; calibration errors up to 44%
column6: English only; correctness judged by an LLM plus heuristics; no participant data of its own; no access to pretraining data

column2: Just Ask for Calibration (Tian, Mitchell, Zhou, Sharma, Rafailov, Yao, Finn, Manning)
column3: How can calibrated confidence be elicited from models tuned with human feedback, whose token probabilities are often poorly calibrated?
column4: Self-verbalized: one- and two-stage numeric and linguistic confidence compared with label probability
column5: Verbalized confidences typically better calibrated than conditional probabilities, often reducing ECE by a relative 50% or more (gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4, claude-1, claude-2, Llama-2-70b-chat; TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA); RLHF generally worsens Llama-2-70B log-probability calibration
column6: Short-form factual QA only; correctness judged by an LLM equivalence check; gains less consistent for Llama-2-70b-chat; claude-1 weaker at verbalizing; venue taken from search listing (EMNLP 2023), not stated on the preprint

column2: Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know (Kapoor, Gruver, Roberts, Collins, Pal, Bhatt, Weller, Dooley, Goldblum, Wilson)
column3: Is prompting enough to obtain calibrated uncertainty, or must it be trained?
column4: Calibration tuning: a probe, LoRA, or LoRA+prompt estimator trained on about 20,000 graded answers from 16 benchmarks, with a divergence regularizer
column5: Mean over six base models: ECE 29.9% to 10.8% and AUROC 70.2% to 71.6% with the regularizer; about 1,000 labeled examples beat simpler baselines; transfers to SelfAware; user study N=181
column6: Needs a second model alongside the answering model; fact-based questions only; calibration worse for some models on a 62-question coding set; user study preliminary; read via a paraphrasing tool, numbers to be spot-checked

column2: INSIDE: LLMs' Internal States Retain the Power of Hallucination Detection (Chen, Liu, Chen, Gu, Wu, Tao, Fu, Ye)
column3: Logit- and consistency-based detection lose semantic information in token decoding
column4: EigenScore on the covariance of sampled responses' embeddings plus test-time feature clipping (white-box, sampling-based)
column5: Higher AUROC than perplexity, length-normalized entropy, and lexical similarity on CoQA, SQuAD, and NQ with LLaMA and OPT models; perplexity does slightly better on TriviaQA (LLaMA-7B CoQA: 80.4 with clipping vs 68.7 for length-normalized entropy); clipping adds at most 1.8 AUROC points
column6: Needs internal states, so no black-box use; needs multiple generations

column2: Revisiting Uncertainty Estimation and Calibration of LLMs (Tao, Yeh, Dong, Huang, Torr, Xu)
column3: How do token-probability, numerical verbalized, and linguistic verbalized uncertainty compare across many models?
column4: Benchmarking three black-box single-pass methods on MMLU-Pro across 80 models (0.6B to 671B)
column5: Linguistic verbalized uncertainty generally strongest on calibration and discrimination
column6: though not for every model; high accuracy does not imply reliable uncertainty; better on reasoning than knowledge-heavy tasks; good calibration does not necessarily give good error ranking
column7: Three single-pass methods and one benchmark; LLM judge assessed only in a small-scale experiment; preprint cited (a NeurIPS 2025 listing was seen, not verified)

column2: Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees (Mohri, Hashimoto)
column3: Can a correctness guarantee be given for free-form LM output?
column4: Conformal prediction over claims: score sub-claims, back off by removing the least certain until the calibrated threshold is met
column5: With GPT-4 on FActScore, NaturalQuestions, MATH: 80-90% correctness guarantees (50 inputs per dataset); introduction reports correctness rising 30% to 80%, 78% to 93%, 75% to 95%; retention of the majority of sub-claims stated in the abstract and introduction, but about half of FActScore sub-claims at the ~80% factuality level in Section 6.2.2
column6: Exchangeability; binary entailment oracle; scores in the experiments come from prompting GPT-4; guarantee on every output may be impossible; text we read stopped partway through Section 4

column2: Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty (Damani, Puri, Slocum, Shenfeld, Choshen, Kim, Andreas)
column3: Can RL teach a model to give calibrated confidence without losing accuracy?
column4: RLCR: correctness reward minus a Brier penalty on verbalized confidence (GRPO)
column5: Qwen2.5-7B on HotpotQA: accuracy 62.1% vs 63.0% for a correctness-only reward; in-domain ECE 0.37 to 0.03; out-of-domain ECE (six datasets) 0.46 to 0.21
column6: Out-of-domain calibration error still high in absolute terms; confidence summed across answers can exceed 1; SFT+RLCR lost out-of-domain accuracy

column2: Can LLMs Learn Uncertainty on Their Own? (Liu, Li, Liu, Zhan, Wong, Chao, Zhang)
column3: Can a model be taught to express uncertainty that matches its own generation uncertainty?
column4: Uncertainty-aware instruction tuning (UaIT) of LLaMA2 and Mistral
column5: Abstract only: 45.2% improvement in uncertainty-expression effectiveness (baseline not stated); reasonable out-of-domain generalization
column6: Only the abstract and proceedings entry were available to us; datasets, baselines, and limitations not stated

column2: Adaptive Retrieval Without Self-Knowledge? (Moskvoretskii, Lysyuk, Salnikov, Ivanov, Pletenev, Galimzianova, Krayko, Konovalov, Nikishina, Panchenko)
column3: Do adaptive-retrieval pipelines beat using an uncertainty score as the retrieval trigger?
column4: Comparison of 8 adaptive-retrieval methods and 27 uncertainty estimators on 6 QA datasets, 10 metrics
column5: Uncertainty triggers comparable on multi-hop and better on single-hop datasets, with fewer retrieval and LM calls, not uniformly (2WikiMultiHopQA: best 0.384 vs 0.454 in-accuracy for AdaptiveRAG); no method dominates all axes
column6: One model (LLaMA 3.1-8b-instruct); six datasets

column2: Agentic Confidence Calibration (Zhang, Xiong, Wu)
column3: How can confidence be calibrated over a whole agent trajectory?
column4: Holistic Trajectory Calibration (HTC): 48 trajectory features, regularized linear model; a general calibrator (GAC) is also proposed
column5: Eight benchmarks
column6: mainly smolagents; reduced variant has the lowest ECE and Brier score on the three datasets in the main table (HLE ECE 0.031 vs 0.656 for verbalized confidence); on HLE the full variant AUROC 0.617 is below a temperature-scaled baseline 0.628
column7: Labels from an LLM judge (reported 90-95% agreement with experts on a subset); GAC results and limitations not in the text we could access

column2: Every Response Counts: Quantifying Uncertainty of LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems through Tensor Decomposition (Chen, Yao, Chen, Papalexakis, Wei)
column3: How can uncertainty be quantified for multi-agent runs?
column4: MATU: embed intermediate outputs of sampled runs, ragged tensor, PARAFAC2, reconstruction loss as score
column5: Highest AUROC and AUARC in the rows we checked across Camel, AutoGen, AnyMac on MATH, MoreHopQA, MMLU (HumanEval only in a tool-use test) (MATH/GPT-4o/Camel: 0.6797 vs 0.5825); margins small in some settings (MoreHopQA/GPT-4o/Camel: 0.5555 vs 0.5480)
column6: Cost grows linearly with sampled runs (10 here); bounded by embedding-model quality

column2: What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know (Steyvers, Tejeda, Kumar, Belem, Karny, Hu, Mayer, Smyth)
column3: Do people's confidence in LLM answers match the models' reliability?
column4: Human study, 301 participants (Prolific), MMLU and TriviaQA, with explanations varied in uncertainty language and length
column5: Model AUC 0.751/0.746/0.781 (GPT-3.5/PaLM2/GPT-4o) vs human 0.589/0.602/0.592; people mainly overconfident on multiple choice; confidence-aligned explanations narrowed both gaps but did not improve participant accuracy in the multiple-choice experiments (AUC pairs differ by question type)
column6: Multiple-choice and short-answer only; explanations needed two prompts; causes untested; no venue found beyond arXiv

column2: Relying on the Unreliable (Zhou, Hwang, Ren, Sap)
column3: How do LMs' confident wording and reluctance to hedge affect user reliance?
column4: Audit of nine LMs on 284 MMLU questions (49 prompts) plus a trivia-game reliance study (25 participants per setting)
column5: Confident-sounding answers wrong 47% of the time on average; users relied on 73% of an overconfident model's incorrect confident answers; performance 76% in miscalibrated vs 86% in calibrated rounds; reward-model scores favor plain statements over uncertain wording
column6: English only; U.S. participants; regex-coded markers; MMLU and capital-city trivia only
